name: Rib flare correction / diaphragm breathing

lead: Rib flare describes lower ribs that stick out forward or sideways, most visible from the side or with the arms raised. Looksmaxxing forums discuss it as something that can spoil the torso silhouette, and correction aims for a smoother, more aligned midsection.

Fitness and physical-therapy writers link it to posture, core weakness and chest-dominant breathing. The approach centres on diaphragmatic breathing and core-bracing drills meant to lower the rib cage over the pelvis; no controlled trial found tests breathing drills for visible rib prominence in healthy people.

paras: People practise slow diaphragmatic breathing, often lying down, with exhalation and core engagement to draw the lower ribs in, then carry it into planks and other trunk work. Changes are described as building over weeks of practice.

The exercises are low-impact and generally regarded as low risk. Flared or prominent ribs can accompany scoliosis, pectus excavatum or other structural conditions, which clinicians assess and manage differently, including surgically in some pectus cases.

web.title: Rib flare correction / diaphragm breathing — Grokipedia

angle.text: Posture communities use diaphragm breathing and core drills to pull protruding lower ribs back in for a cleaner torso line. Proponents link rib flare to weak core and breathing mechanics; direct trials on appearance are almost absent.

lead: Rib flare is a descriptive term, used mainly in physical therapy, fitness and posture communities, for lower ribs that protrude outward or forward rather than sitting flush with the abdomen. It is generally described as a postural pattern rather than a disease, although similar-looking rib cage prominence can accompany structural conditions such as scoliosis or pectus excavatum.[1][1]

Rib flare correction refers to exercises, chiefly diaphragmatic breathing combined with core engagement and posture work, intended to bring the lower ribs down and back. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed alongside pectus excavatum as a torso-aesthetics concern.

No clinical trial found has tested breathing exercises specifically for reducing visible rib flare. Related literature consists of radiographic measurement studies of rib cage deformity in scoliosis, clinical commentary on respiratory exercises for asymmetrical trunk posture, and surgical series on pectus repair.[2][3][4]

paras: Descriptions of rib flare, mostly from physical-therapy and fitness writing, characterise it as the lower ribs (roughly ribs 7 to 10) angling outward and upward, creating a visible edge at the front or side of the torso, sometimes on one side only.[1] Grokipedia's summary lists suggested contributing factors including weak core muscles, prolonged sitting, chest-dominant breathing, stress-related breathing patterns, genetics and postpartum changes, and notes that it is not generally painful on its own.[1]
The infrasternal angle, the angle at which the costal margins meet at the front, is sometimes used to describe a wide or narrow lower rib cage.[1]

According to the physical-therapy explanation summarised in Grokipedia, the diaphragm attaches to the inner surface of the lower ribs, and the abdominal wall muscles (transversus abdominis and obliques) attach to the costal margin. When breathing relies on the upper chest and accessory muscles, or when the abdominals are not engaged, the lower ribs are said to ride up and out, shrinking the zone of apposition, the region where the diaphragm lies against the inner rib cage.[1]

A clinical commentary in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy describes a pattern of asymmetry involving the trunk, ribs, spine, pelvis and hips, and presents a side-lying respiratory exercise combined with a hip adductor pull-back as a way to address it.[5] It is a clinical application paper rather than a controlled trial.

In general terms, practitioners describe diaphragmatic or three-dimensional breathing that expands the lower ribs sideways and back while keeping the front of the rib cage down, paired with abdominal engagement during exhalation and exercises such as planks and dead bugs. Hands-on techniques and postural awareness are also mentioned in physical-therapy descriptions.[1] Individual programmes vary widely and are not standardised.
No studies found testing breathing or core exercises as a means of reducing visible rib flare in otherwise healthy people.

Related research includes a 2026 study proposing a radiographic measurement called rib flare distance to quantify axial rib cage deformity in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, reported as highly reliable; this concerns measurement of a structural deformity, not an exercise outcome.[3] A 2024 paper in Heliyon examined markerless 3D pose estimation from a single camera for quantifying exercise movement, and is a technology study rather than a test of rib flare correction.[2] A 2026 retrospective series of 72 pectus patients described surgical bridging-bar techniques for aesthetic and functional results.[4]

Rib cage prominence can accompany scoliosis, where it is associated with pulmonary function and cosmetic appearance according to the rib flare distance study, and pectus excavatum, a sunken breastbone.[3][1] Clinicians treat these through assessment and, where indicated, bracing or surgery. Exercise-based rib flare programmes are described in the sources as aimed at postural rib position, not at these structural conditions.

A long guide on looksmax.org covers fixing pectus excavatum and rib flare, with sections on what the conditions are, proposed solutions and cited studies. Its author describes having pectus himself and writes for others dealing with it. Discussion in these communities treats the rib cage as part of torso proportion and shirtless appearance.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, rib flare is usually discussed together with pectus excavatum as a correctable torso flaw, with guides proposing exercise-based fixes.
